Hook: On the second of April 2025, the President of the United States stood in the Rose Garden with a board of countries and numbers. Imports from almost every country would pay a tariff of at least ten percent, and more from countries the United States bought more from than it sold to. The numbers came from one formula, published that evening by the Trade Representative. The tariff on a country is the bilateral deficit, imports minus exports, divided by imports, and by two parameters: epsilon, how strongly imports fall when their price rises, set at four; and phi, the share of a tariff that reaches import prices, set at a quarter. Four times a quarter is one, so they cancel. The result was then halved, with a floor of ten percent.

Take Vietnam. In 2024 the United States imported about a hundred and thirty-seven billion dollars of goods from Vietnam and sold it about thirteen. The deficit over imports is 90 percent. Halved, 45; the published rate was 46. Within days economists were arguing about phi. The evidence from the 2018 tariffs, which this part will show, is that tariffs reached import prices almost one for one. Kevin Corinth and Stan Veuger pointed out that with phi near 0.95, the same formula gives about 12 percent. One parameter, a factor of four. And a deeper question: does a bilateral deficit measure anything a tariff should fix?

Before the evidence, each side's best case, as its most careful defenders would make it. For: some supplies, chips, medicines, rare minerals, should not depend on a rival that can cut them off; a tariff is leverage in negotiations; it raises revenue; and the places the China shock of Part thirty-six left behind deserve protection. Against: the tariff is paid mostly by buyers at home; partners retaliate; labour and capital move into what the country does relatively badly; and an overall trade deficit is set by how much a country saves and invests, which a tariff barely touches. This part puts each claim to the data and the models.

The question: what happens to the gains from trade when trade becomes a weapon? Who paid for the tariffs of 2018 and 2025? When do tariff wars start, and why does anyone sign a trade agreement? What does a bilateral deficit measure? How does dependence on a supplier become power over you, and what is resilience worth? And when does industrial policy work?
Economics, Built. Part sixty-six: geoeconomics and industrial policy.

Part sixty-five asked what machines will do to the economy. This part asks what states do with it. By the end you will know what the tariffs of 2018 and 2025 did to prices, trade and welfare; why countries are tempted into tariff wars, and why trade agreements exist; how to run tariffs through the quantitative trade model of Part thirty-six, and what a bilateral deficit does and does not mean; how interdependence becomes a weapon, and what resilience is worth; and when industrial policy has worked, from Napoleon's blockade to South Korea's heavy industry, and when subsidies become a race.
Record: Chapter one. What the tariffs did.

In 2018 and 2019 the United States raised tariffs on washing machines, solar panels, steel, aluminium and then most imports from China, and its partners retaliated. Mary Amiti, Stephen Redding and David Weinstein, and separately Pablo Fajgelbaum and coauthors, looked at the prices foreign sellers charged before the tariff. They did not fall. The whole tariff reached American buyers. By the end of 2018, Amiti and her coauthors estimated, Americans were paying three point two billion dollars a month in tariffs, and losing another one point four billion a month of real income to the trade that no longer happened. Fajgelbaum and coauthors put the loss to buyers of imports at fifty-one billion dollars a year; after counting the tariff revenue and the gains to protected producers, the net loss was seven point two billion, four hundredths of one percent of GDP. Small, because most of it was a transfer. And Aaron Flaaen and Justin Pierce found that manufacturing industries more exposed to the tariffs lost jobs relative to others: the dearer inputs and the retaliation outweighed the protection.

The second round was larger. Here is the effective tariff rate: the customs duties the United States collected each quarter, over its imports of goods. About 1.6 percent in 2017; 3.5 percent at the end of the first round. In 2025 it rose from 2.8 percent to 11.3 percent by the end of the year, the highest since the Second World War. In February 2026 the Supreme Court ruled, six to three, that the emergency-powers law used for most of the new tariffs did not allow tariffs at all. Tariffs under other laws remained, and by the third quarter of 2026 the rate was 6.8 percent.

Who paid this time? In orange, the prices foreign sellers charged at the border, before the tariff, excluding food and fuel. They did not fall in 2025: they rose about 1 percent. Foreign sellers did not absorb the tariff; as in 2018, it was paid at the American border. In green, the consumer prices of goods other than food and energy: down 0.7 percent in 2024, up 1.4 percent in 2025. The rise reached shoppers slowly. Alberto Cavallo, Paola Llamas and Franco Vazquez tracked daily prices in large American retailers: by September 2025 about a fifth of the tariff had reached the prices of imported goods on the shelves, adding about seven tenths of a point to the consumer price index. The rest was, for the moment, absorbed by importers and retailers in their margins.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: a tariff arrives.

Your turn. You set America's trade policy for ten rounds, a round a year, against the rest of the world as one partner. Each round, the model of chapter four gives your real income. Both at free trade: zero. A twenty-five percent tariff while the partner keeps free trade: you gain 0.48 percent, because you pay less for what you import. The partner taxes you and you do not: you lose 0.89. Both tax: you lose 0.59. You have three plans: free trade throughout; a tariff, kept; or a tariff for two rounds, then back to free trade. And you do not know your partner. It may copy your last move, it may never retaliate, or it may retaliate for ever once taxed. Each is equally likely, and next year counts nine tenths as much as this one. Which plan?

Here is what each plan earns against each partner. Free trade throughout earns zero against everyone: nothing gained, nothing lost. A tariff kept earns 3.1 percent of a year's income against a partner who never retaliates, but against the other two, who answer and keep answering, it loses 2.8. A tariff for two rounds is worst against the partner who never forgives: you pay the war, then free trade on your side while they keep their tariff. Averaged over the three partners, free trade wins. A tariff pays only if you are sure your partner will not answer, and partners learn. That is the logic of the trade agreements in the next chapter.
Games: Chapter three. Trade wars as games.

Start with why a tariff tempts a large country. In the model, the United States puts a uniform tariff on everyone else, and nobody answers. Its real income rises at first. The tariff cuts what Americans buy abroad, the world price of those goods falls, and part of the tariff is paid by foreigners: the terms of trade improve. Up to a point: the gain peaks at a tariff of about 25 percent, the optimal tariff, roughly one over the elasticity of foreign supply. The rest of the world loses more than America gains. A large country's tariff is a way of taking a slice of other people's income, at a cost to the world.

But the rest of the world can do the same. For each tariff the other side sets, find each side's best answer. America's, in blue, is the same whatever the rest does: about 25 percent. The rest of the world's, in orange, is about the same. Where the two cross is the Nash equilibrium of the tariff war: each taxing the other at about 25 percent. And there, America is 0.59 percent poorer than at free trade, and the rest of the world 0.17 percent. Each did the best it could given the other, and both lost. It is Part eleven's prisoners' dilemma, with countries.

This is the modern economic theory of trade agreements, from Kyle Bagwell and Robert Staiger. Each country lowers its tariff because the other does: reciprocity turns the prisoners' dilemma into a deal. The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, from 1947, and the World Trade Organization after it, added bound tariffs that cannot be raised at will, the same tariff for every member, and a court for disputes. How much is at stake? Ralph Ossa computed the Nash tariffs of a model of the world economy: they average sixty-three percent, and a breakdown of cooperation would cost governments two point nine percent of income on average. Cooperation held for seventy years for the reason of Part eleven's folk theorem: the game is repeated, and a deviation today is answered tomorrow.
Model: Chapter four. A fifteen percent tariff in the quantitative model.

Now a tariff in the quantitative model of Part thirty-six, by exact hat algebra. Each country's spending share on each supplier changes with the supplier's wage and the tariff, raised to minus theta. The world is thirteen economies: the twelve largest and the rest, with their trade flows of 2019 from CEPII. The tariff revenue goes back to the country that collects it. The United States is about a quarter of world spending and imports about 11 percent of what it spends. We set deficits to zero first, as the literature does, so that a deficit held fixed by assumption does not drive the answer; and we try three trade elasticities, because the evidence of chapter one says it is small in the short run and larger later.

Impose a uniform fifteen percent tariff on all American imports. With no retaliation and theta of four, American real income rises 0.42 percent: the terms of trade again. The partners lose 0.18 percent. The gain is largest when trade responds least, because then foreigners cannot escape the tax. Now let every partner answer with fifteen percent on American goods. America's gain becomes a loss: -0.29 percent at theta of four, and larger when trade is more responsive. American imports fall by 27 percent without retaliation and 48 with it. The numbers are small as shares of income, as Fajgelbaum and coauthors found, because trade is a modest share of a large economy; they are large for the industries and places that trade.

Who pays, in the model? In the long run, about 48 percent of the tariff is borne abroad, through lower wages and prices in the countries America buys from. In the data, in the first year or two of both rounds, foreigners bore almost none of it. The two are not in contradiction. Most American imports are priced in dollars, and those prices are sticky, as Part thirty-four showed; and trade responds slowly: Christoph Boehm, Andrei Levchenko and Nitya Pandalai-Nayar estimate an elasticity of about three quarters in the first year and about two after a decade. The terms-of-trade gain the optimal-tariff argument relies on, if it comes, comes late, and only if nobody retaliates.
Power: Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman argued in 2019 that globalization did not produce a flat network of equals. It produced hubs: the dollar's clearing banks, the messaging system SWIFT, a few cloud providers, a few chip foundries. Countries connect to each other through them. A state that controls a hub gains two powers. The panopticon: it sees every transaction that passes through. And the chokepoint: it can cut a country off. In 2012 Iranian banks were disconnected from SWIFT's messages. In 2022, after the invasion of Ukraine, about three hundred billion dollars of the Russian central bank's reserves held abroad were frozen. Interdependence, which economists had seen as a source of peace, had become a weapon.

How much power does dependence give? Part thirty-six's formula for the gains from trade answers it. If a share s of your spending goes to one supplier's goods, and it cuts you off, your real income falls by one minus one minus s to the power one over theta. At a fifth of spending and theta of four, that is 5.4 percent of income, every year the cutoff lasts. It is much larger when the goods are hard to replace, low theta, and small when other suppliers can step in. That loss is the most a supplier can demand from you by threatening a cutoff: a concession worth more than the loss, and you would rather be cut off. Which is why the goods that matter for power are the ones with few suppliers and no substitutes: rare earths, advanced chips, some medicines.

Christopher Clayton, Matteo Maggiori and Jesse Schreger built this into a framework. A hegemon at the centre of many networks, finance, technology, trade, can tie them together: a threat in one to win something in another. A target complies when the loss it is threatened with exceeds what it is asked to give, and it hedges, diversifying away from the hegemon, at a cost. From the world's point of view the hedging is waste: the fear of cutoffs makes everyone poorer even when no cutoff happens. And targets answer by building their own hubs: payment systems, reserve assets, suppliers. Chapter eleven returns to the most important of them, the dollar.
Resilience: Resilience has a price. A firm buys an input from a cheap foreign supplier, 10 percent cheaper, who is cut off with a probability of 5 percent a year. A cutoff hurts more the more the firm depends on it. Here is the firm's expected cost, as it varies the share it buys abroad. It chooses about 50 percent. But a cutoff also hurts the firm's customers and workers, who are not in its sums. Counting them, society's expected cost is the red curve, and society would buy only 25 percent abroad. Gene Grossman, Elhanan Helpman and Hugo Lhuillier show how delicate the real case is: with some demand structures firms buy too little resilience, with others too much, and a subsidy to diversify can beat bringing production home. Note what even the simple case does not say: the right share is not zero. Security is bought at the margin, not by leaving trade.

The reallocation is already under way. Laura Alfaro and Davin Chor measured China's share of American goods imports: twenty-one point six percent at its peak in 2017, sixteen point five in 2022, and in their later work about nine percent by the middle of 2025, after the new tariffs. The share went to Vietnam, Mexico and others. It was not free: the unit values of what America bought from Vietnam rose about ten percent, from Mexico about three. And much of what comes from the new suppliers is still made with Chinese parts. Friend-shoring buys some security, at a price, and less of it than the bilateral numbers suggest.
Infant: Chapter eight. Industrial policy, the old case.

Industrial policy is older than free trade theory's victory. In 1791 Alexander Hamilton told Congress that a young country's manufacturers could not compete at first with Britain's established ones, and should be protected and encouraged until they could. Fifty years later Friedrich List added that Britain itself had climbed behind tariffs and then preached free trade, kicking away the ladder. The economics behind the argument is learning by doing: an industry's costs fall as it produces, so a firm that starts today is cheaper tomorrow.

Here is a model of it. An industry starts with costs sixty percent above the world price. Behind a 60 percent tariff for 10 years, it can sell at home, and as it produces, its costs fall. After that the tariff goes, and it survives only if it can beat the world price. With slow learning, in red, costs fall, but not far enough: when the tariff goes, the industry dies. With faster learning, in gold, it just makes it. With fast learning, in green, it ends well below the world price, and exports.

Economists have two old tests. John Stuart Mill's: the protected industry must eventually survive without protection. The slow learner fails it. Charles Bastable's is stricter: the gains, once the industry beats the world price, must outweigh the costs of protecting it while it learned, both discounted. The middle case survives, but at a ten percent discount rate its gains do not repay what it cost. Only the fast learner passes both. And Robert Baldwin added a third. If the learning stays inside the firm, the firm could borrow to pay for its early losses, and needs no tariff. Policy is justified only when the learning spills over, to other firms, workers or suppliers, which no lender can be repaid for. Which raises the empirical question: has it ever worked?
Dials: Chapter twelve. The Dials: who pays, and what a war costs.

Two Dials. The first is pass-through, first opened in Part thirty-four. For exchange rates, little of a currency move reaches American import prices when they are set in dollars, nearly all when they are set in the exporter's currency, and this film's own estimate is 0.44 after a year. For the tariffs of 2018 and 2019, Amiti and her coauthors and Fajgelbaum and his found complete pass-through to the prices American buyers paid at the border. And for 2025, at the next stage, the shelf: about a fifth of the tariff had reached retail prices by September, in Cavallo and coauthors' daily data. The status: depends on the setting. At the border, tariffs are paid by American buyers; how much reaches consumers, and how fast, depends on margins, competition and time.

The second Dial is new: the cost of a tariff war, from cooperation to the tariffs each country would choose alone. Ossa's model of the world economy: 2.9 percent of income on average, with lobbying pushing tariffs up. This film's two-bloc war: 0.59 percent for the United States, 0.17 percent for the rest of the world. The status: depends on the setting. More trade, and more political pressure, make a war costlier. And in every model, the gain from a tariff lasts only while others do not answer.
Practice: Chapter thirteen. In practice: ministries, supply chains, sanctions.

Forecasting what tariffs do to prices is a job, and it starts with a call. Called it? In June 2025 the median member of the Federal Reserve's policy committee projected core inflation of 3.1 percent for 2025, up from 2.8 in March, as the tariffs reached prices. The outcome: core prices rose 2.8 percent from the end of 2024 to the end of 2025. Goods prices did turn up, but the tariffs reached shelves slowly, and some were cut or suspended. Partly right: the direction, not the size. The lesson of chapter one, again: a tariff's effect on inflation depends on how fast it travels from the border to the shelf.

Where is this used? In trade ministries, which score a tariff or an agreement with quantitative models like chapter four's: revenue, prices, and who gains and loses. In budget offices, which score a tariff's revenue net of the imports it stops and the income it lowers, Part fifty-eight's craft. In companies, which price chapter seven's trade-off for themselves: a second supplier, larger inventories, where to build the next factory. And in sanctions compliance, where banks and firms screen every payment and shipment against government lists: the hub's power, run by the hub's users.

Three cautions from this part. A tariff is a tax, paid mostly at home, at least in the first years; any gain from the terms of trade comes late and invites answers. A bilateral balance is not a scorecard: the overall balance is saving minus investment, and the bilateral ones mostly reflect who is good at what. And industrial policy needs a test: temporary, disciplined by having to sell abroad, aimed at learning that spills over, and evaluated by a design, not by the industry's own account.
